main.prompt: What does EU stand for?
main.explanation: EU is simply short for European Union — a group of countries in Europe that work together.
main.tip: The letters are the words: E for European, U for Union.

main.prompt: Which sentence best describes the European Union?
main.explanation: The EU is a group of separate countries that cooperate and make SOME decisions together. It is not one country, it is not worldwide, and it is not an army.
main.tip: Think "team," not "country." The players stay separate — they just agree to play together.
choices: A group of European countries that cooperate and make some decisions together.
One single country that replaced all the countries of Europe.
A club for countries on every continent.
An army that fights for Europe.

main.prompt: What continent is the European Union in?
main.explanation: Every EU member country is in Europe — that is why it is called the EUROPEAN Union.
main.tip: The answer is hiding in the name: EUROPEan Union.

main.prompt: How many member countries does the EU have today?
main.explanation: The EU has 27 member countries today. It had 28 until the United Kingdom left.
main.tip: 28 members minus the UK leaves 27.

main.prompt: Even though EU countries work together, what does each country still keep?
main.explanation: The 27 countries cooperate, but each one still has its own government, culture, and traditions.
main.tip: Joining a team does not erase who you are — every country keeps its own name, food, language, and government.
choices: Its own government, culture, and traditions.
Nothing — the EU controls everything about each country.
Only its flag, and nothing else.

main.prompt: Fill in the blank: The EU works together for peace, trade, and ______.
main.explanation: The worksheet's sentence is "The EU works together for peace, trade, and cooperation."
main.tip: Co-operation = operating together. It's the whole reason the EU exists.
main.hint: Write the one-word term from the worksheet.

main.prompt: After major wars in Europe, what did many European countries want?
main.explanation: After terrible wars, many European countries wanted peace and a better future, so they decided to work together instead of fighting.
main.tip: The EU was born out of war. Countries that had been fighting chose to sit at a table instead.
choices: More fighting to settle old arguments.
To stop trading with each other.

main.prompt: "Peace through cooperation" means that countries decided to…
main.explanation: Countries met together and decided to work together instead of fighting — cooperation was the path to peace.
main.tip: Cooperation = co-operate = operate together. Working together is the opposite of fighting.
choices: build bigger armies than their neighbors.
each solve their problems completely alone.

main.prompt: Select ALL of the reasons countries joined the EU.
main.explanation: Countries joined for peace, trade, travel, jobs, and being stronger together. No country gave up its own government — that is the one that does not belong.
main.tip: Five reasons, and all five are things that HELP people: Peace, Trade, Travel, Jobs, Stronger Together.
choices: Peace — less conflict and a safer future
Trade — easier to buy and sell goods across countries
Travel — easier to visit, study, and explore other countries
To replace every country's own government with one ruler

main.prompt: The EU makes it easier for people — especially young people — to find work in other member countries. Which reason for joining is that?
main.explanation: "Jobs" means more opportunities for people, especially young people, because they can work in other member countries.
main.tip: Jobs = opportunities to WORK. Travel = visiting. Trade = goods being bought and sold.

main.prompt: "Countries can solve big challenges better as a team." Which reason for joining does this describe?
main.explanation: "Stronger Together" is the idea that big problems are easier to solve as a group than alone.
main.tip: One country pushing a heavy door is slow; 27 pushing together is fast.

main.prompt: In what year did the EU start, with just 6 countries?
main.explanation: The EU started in 1957 with 6 countries and grew as more countries joined.
main.tip: Its growth line is 6 → 9 → 27: six in 1957, nine by 1973, twenty-seven today.

main.prompt: How many countries did the EU begin with?
main.explanation: It began with 6 countries: France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.
main.tip: 6 to start, 9 by 1973, 27 today. The team kept growing.

main.prompt: Put the EU's growth in order, from earliest to most recent.
main.explanation: The EU began in 1957 with 6 founding countries, reached 9 by 1973, kept growing through the 1980s–2000s, and has 27 members today.
main.tip: The number only goes up: 6, 9, more, 27.

main.prompt: Select ALL of the countries that were among the original 6 founding members.
main.explanation: The founding six were France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. Poland joined much later, in the 1980s–2000s wave.
main.tip: The first six sit together in the middle of the map: the three big ones (France, Germany, Italy) plus three small neighbors (Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg).

main.prompt: By 1973, the EU had grown from 6 countries to how many?
main.explanation: By 1973 the EU had grown to 9 countries. More joined during the 1980s–2000s, reaching 27 today.
main.tip: 6 → 9 → 27. The 1973 step adds three.

main.prompt: Name any ONE country that is a member of the EU today.
main.explanation: Any of the 27 members counts: France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland, Greece, Ireland, Sweden and 19 others. The United Kingdom does NOT count, because it left in 2020.
main.tip: If you are not sure, picture the word bank from the worksheet: France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland, Greece — all six are members.
main.hint: Write one country name. Careful — the UK is no longer a member.
main.display: Any of the 27 members — for example France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland, or Greece

main.prompt: Greece, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Malta and Cyprus are grouped into which region of the EU?
main.explanation: These are the Southern Europe members — the sunny, Mediterranean side of the EU.
main.tip: Southern Europe = the warm coastlines on the Mediterranean Sea. Sun, beaches, and ancient history.

main.prompt: Which of these EU countries is in Central & Eastern Europe?
main.explanation: Poland is in Central & Eastern Europe, along with countries like Czechia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia and the Baltic states.
main.tip: Central & Eastern Europe is the right-hand side of the EU map — Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Romania.

main.prompt: Match each EU country to its region.
main.explanation: Sweden sits with the Western & Northern members, Greece with the Southern (Mediterranean) members, and Poland with Central & Eastern Europe.
main.tip: Picture the map: cold north-west, sunny south, and the eastern half of the union.

main.prompt: Which of these EU countries is in Western & Northern Europe?
main.explanation: Sweden is in Western & Northern Europe, with Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
main.tip: Western & Northern = the top-left of the map, where it is colder: Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Ireland.

main.prompt: Name one EU country in Southern Europe.
main.explanation: The Southern Europe members are Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta, Portugal, and Spain.
main.tip: Southern Europe borders the Mediterranean: Italy's boot, Greece's islands, Spain and Portugal, plus the island nations Malta and Cyprus.
main.display: Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta, Portugal, or Spain

main.prompt: What does the word "Brexit" come from?
main.explanation: "Brexit" is a shorter name for the United Kingdom leaving the EU: BRitain + EXIT.
main.tip: Say it slowly — BR-EXIT. The word itself spells out Britain exiting.

main.prompt: In what year did people in the United Kingdom vote on whether to stay in or leave the EU?
main.explanation: The vote took place in 2016. The UK did not actually leave until January 31, 2020.
main.tip: Two dates, four years apart: the VOTE was 2016, the EXIT was 2020.

main.prompt: Put the Brexit events in the order they happened.
main.explanation: The 2016 vote came first, 'Leave' won 52% to 48%, the UK officially left on January 31 2020, and the EU dropped from 28 members to 27.
main.tip: Vote, result, exit, new total — cause and effect, in that order.
items: The UK votes on leaving the EU
The UK officially leaves the EU
The EU is left with 27 members

main.prompt: What percentage voted 'Leave' in the 2016 vote?
main.explanation: 'Leave' won with 52%, and 'Stay' had 48%. The vote was close — only 4 points apart.
main.tip: 52 and 48 add up to 100, and they are only 4 apart. It was nearly a tie.

main.prompt: What percentage voted to stay in the EU?
main.explanation: 'Stay' received 48% of the vote, just behind 'Leave' at 52%.
main.tip: Leave 52, Stay 48. The bigger number won, but barely.

main.prompt: On what date did the United Kingdom officially leave the EU?
main.explanation: The UK officially left the EU on January 31, 2020 — about four years after the 2016 vote.
main.tip: The last day of January, 2020. Vote in 2016, leave on 1/31/2020.
main.hint: Write the full date (month, day, year).

main.prompt: After leaving the EU, the United Kingdom stopped trading with European countries entirely.
main.explanation: False. The UK no longer helps make EU rules, but it still trades, travels, and cooperates with European countries.
main.tip: Leaving the team is not leaving the neighborhood. They stopped making the rules, not being neighbors.

main.prompt: Which statement describes the UK before Brexit, when it was still in the EU?
main.explanation: Before Brexit, the UK sat at the table — it helped make EU rules and had a say in EU decisions.
main.tip: Before = inside the room where the rules get made. After = outside that room.
choices: The UK helped make EU rules and had a say in EU decisions.
The UK had no say in any EU decisions.
The UK was not allowed to trade with Europe.
The UK had already left the EU.

main.prompt: Which statement describes the UK after Brexit?
main.explanation: After leaving, the UK no longer helps make EU rules — but it still trades, travels, and cooperates with European countries.
main.tip: Leaving the team does not mean leaving the neighborhood. They stopped making the rules, not being friends.
choices: The UK no longer helps make EU rules, but it still trades and works with Europe.
The UK no longer has any contact with European countries.
The UK still votes on all EU decisions.
The UK became part of a different continent.

main.prompt: Is the United Kingdom a member of the EU today?
main.explanation: The UK is no longer a member of the EU. It left on January 31, 2020, which is why the EU now has 27 members instead of 28.
main.tip: If the UK were still in, the EU would have 28. The number 27 is proof that it left.
choices: No — it left and is no longer a member.

main.prompt: Money: The UK paid membership fees to the EU. What did supporters of leaving want to happen with that money?
main.explanation: Supporters of leaving argued the UK paid fees to the EU, and they wanted more of that money spent inside the UK instead.
main.tip: The picture on the sheet was a UK piggy bank next to a fee bill — keep the money at home.
choices: They wanted more of it spent inside the UK.
They wanted to pay the EU even more.
They wanted to give it to other EU countries.
They wanted to stop using money completely.

main.prompt: Trade: What did supporters of leaving want the UK to be able to do?
main.explanation: EU membership made trade with EU countries easier, but supporters of leaving wanted the UK to make its own trade deals with countries around the world.
main.tip: The picture showed a UK ship sailing from Europe out toward THE WORLD — trading wider, not stopping trade.
choices: Make its own trade deals with countries around the world.
Stop trading with every country on Earth.
Trade only with EU countries and no one else.
Let the EU choose all of the UK's trade partners forever.

main.prompt: Movement of labor: EU citizens could live and work in other EU countries. What worried some UK citizens about this?
main.explanation: Because EU citizens could live and work in any member country, some UK citizens worried about job competition and lower-cost labor.
main.tip: "Labor" means work. This argument was about who gets the jobs.
choices: That no one would ever visit the UK.
That UK citizens could not travel anywhere.
That there were too few workers in Europe.

main.prompt: Human rights and laws: What did some UK citizens believe about EU rules?
main.explanation: Some UK citizens believed EU rules limited the UK's control over its own laws, including decisions about deporting foreign-born criminals.
main.tip: This argument is about CONTROL — who gets the final say over British law, London or the EU.
choices: That EU rules limited the UK's control over its own laws.
That the UK had too much control over EU laws.
That the EU had no rules at all.
That EU rules only applied to trade.
